level-1.title: How interest is worked out

story.title: The golden swan
text: A swan whose feathers were solid gold began landing at a poor family's house. Each visit it left one feather behind and flew away again. The family sold the feathers one by one, and for the first time they were not short.
The mother grew impatient. A feather at a time seemed slow when the whole bird was standing there.
The next time it landed she caught it and pulled out every feather at once.
In her hands they turned to ordinary white feathers. The bare swan recovered, flew away, and never returned.
story.moral: The feathers were the interest and the swan was the amount that produced them. Spending the interest leaves the source intact and it keeps producing. Spending the source ends both, and the ending is permanent.

summary: The interest rate is written as a percent for one year.
5 percent means the bank adds ₹5 for every ₹100 you keep.
If you keep ₹1000 at 5 percent, after one year you have ₹1050.
Interest also works the other way. If you borrow, you pay interest.
A higher rate is good when you save. A higher rate is bad when you borrow.

questions.prompt: You keep ₹2000 in an account at 5 percent interest for one year. How much will you have at the end?

image.alt: A bar growing slightly taller, labelled two thousand rupees

questions.hint: 5 percent of 2000 is 100. Add that to the original amount.

questions.prompt: Two rates are on offer: 3% and 9%. Person A is saving money in an account. Person B is borrowing money for a loan. Which rate should each person prefer, and why?

image.alt: A saver and a borrower each facing two different interest rates

options.label: Both should prefer 9%, since higher is always better
Both should prefer 3%, since lower is always safer
A should prefer 9% (more earned); B should prefer 3% (less owed)

questions.hint: A higher rate benefits whoever is receiving interest, and costs whoever is paying it.

questions.prompt: You put ₹800 into an account. After a year at 5 percent interest, you have ₹840. What is the ₹800 called, and what is the ₹40?

image.alt: A starting stack of coins beside a smaller added stack

options.label: Both amounts are called principal
₹800 is the principal; ₹40 is the interest earned
₹800 is the interest; ₹40 is the principal

questions.hint: The principal is what you started with, before anything was added.

level-2.title: Compound interest and time

story.title: The rice on the chessboard
text: A sage brought the game of chess to his king. The king was so taken with it that he offered the sage any reward he cared to name.

The sage asked for rice. One grain on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, and so on - doubling on every square, to the sixty-fourth. The king thought the request almost insulting in its smallness, and agreed at once.

The first row cost him nothing worth counting. By the tenth square the pile was 512 grains, about a handful. By the twenty-first it was around ten lakh grains - a few sacks, and still nothing to a king.

Then the board turned. The thirty-second square alone needed about 215 crore grains. And thirty-two was only halfway. The sixty-fourth square needed more than nine followed by eighteen zeros, and the whole board came to roughly 461 billion tonnes - more rice than the world grows in nine hundred years.
The king could not pay. He had agreed to the shape of the thing without working out where it went.
story.moral: Nothing dramatic happens for the first twenty squares, and that is exactly why doubling gets underestimated. Compound interest has the same shape: the money earns, then the earnings earn, and most of the growth arrives late. So the lever that matters most is not the rate - it is how long the money is left alone.

summary: Simple interest is paid only on the money you first put in.
Compound interest is paid on your money and on the interest already earned.
₹10,000 at 8 percent compound becomes about ₹21,600 after ten years.
Starting early matters more than starting with a large amount.
Credit cards charge compound interest too. Unpaid balances grow quickly.

questions.prompt: ₹1000 grows at 10 percent a year. After year one it is ₹1100. If the interest is COMPOUND, what happens in year two?

image.alt: A curve rising faster over two years

options.label: No further interest is earned after year one
You earn 10% of ₹1000 again, exactly the same as year one
You earn 10% of ₹1100, not just of the original ₹1000

questions.hint: Compound interest is paid on the new, larger total - not the original amount.

questions.prompt: Person A saves ₹500 a month starting at age 15. Person B saves ₹1000 a month but starts at age 25, and both stop at 35. Whose final amount benefits more from compounding, and why might it be closer than expected?

image.alt: Two timelines, one ten years longer than the other

options.label: They will always end with exactly the same amount
Person B - saving twice as much each month always wins
Person A - the extra 10 years lets compounding work for far longer, even saving less each month

questions.hint: Compounding needs TIME above almost everything else, as the lesson stresses.

questions.prompt: You owe ₹5000 on a credit card at a high compound rate and pay nothing for two billing cycles in a row. What happens to the amount you owe between the first and second cycle?

image.alt: A card bill with a rising amount across two cycles

options.label: It grows faster in the second cycle, because interest is now charged on the first cycle's interest too
It stops growing after the first cycle
It grows by the same fixed amount each cycle

questions.hint: Just like savings, compound interest builds on the previous total - but here that total is a debt.

level-3.title: Loans, EMIs and the Rule of 72
summary: A loan is interest working against you. The same compounding that grows savings also grows a debt.
An EMI is an equal monthly payment that repays the loan and its interest together.
Total cost of a loan = EMI × number of months. The difference from what you borrowed is what the loan really costs.
A "flat" rate charges interest on the full amount for the whole loan, even as you pay it down. It costs far more than the same rate on a reducing balance.
The Rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly rate to find roughly how many years money takes to double. At 8%, about 9 years.
It works for debt too. A loan at 24% a year that is never paid doubles in about 3 years.

questions.prompt: You borrow ₹10,000 and pay an EMI of ₹950 for 12 months. How much does the loan cost you in interest?

image.alt: Monthly payments stacked up beside the amount borrowed

questions.hint: Multiply the EMI by the months, then take away what you borrowed.

questions.prompt: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 6% a year?

image.alt: A pile of money doubling over time

options.label: About 6 years
About 72 years
About 12 years

questions.prompt: Two loans both say 12% a year. One charges it on the full amount the whole time (flat). The other charges only on what you still owe (reducing). Which costs more?

image.alt: Two loan offers with the same rate printed on them

options.label: The flat-rate loan, because you pay interest on money you have already paid back
They cost the same, because the rate is the same
The reducing-balance loan

questions.hint: On which loan does the interest shrink as you pay it off?
